answer.diagnosis: Most hidden units are spatially structured size detectors. Small-blob units (0, 3, 5, 8, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23, 24, 25, 28, 31) have a positive centre and a negative ring at the large-blob radius. Large-blob units (1, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16, 27, 30) have a positive annulus. Layer-1 unit 19 is the exception. Every one of its 576 weights is positive, averaging about 50 (about 0.07 each), and the weights have no spatial structure. Its centre weights are even slightly lower than the periphery (for example (11,12)=3 and (12,12)=1, against about 55 at the borders). So it does not measure the blob. It measures the overall brightness of the background. With this summed weight it is by far the strongest layer-1 unit, an always-on global intensity meter. It feeds strongly into layer-2 units u13 and u15, which push toward 'large', and also into u0, u9 and u12. Uniform weights that skip the blob are what a learned background-brightness or global-intensity shortcut looks like, not a size feature. The fix replaces unit 19 with a constant: its input weights are zeroed, and its bias is set to its approximate mean activation. This is about 11.8 in real units, assuming a mean pixel value near 0.29; that value is an estimate. Downstream layer-2 units therefore keep roughly the same operating point. Size discrimination is left to the centre-surround units.

edits.reason: replace with approx mean activation to keep layer-2 calibration
